findings.statement: Heuristic 11, SPOT, with heuristic 10, invariants enforced, and heuristic 12, structured data. CostRecoverySolution (finance.py:375-452) stores each solve outcome twice: feasible (bool) duplicates binding (str), and representative_outlay_gbp, saving_vs_baseline_gbp and saving_pct duplicate outlay.representative fields. Its docstrings call these 'Invariant:' (419, 428, 434), but __post_init__ (443-452) checks only binding's membership and the rate's range. Measured: CostRecoverySolution(feasible=True, binding='infeasible_above_retail', representative_outlay_gbp=999.0, outlay=<rep outlay 66.15>, ...) constructs without error. BillBreakdown in the same file enforces its one identity at construction, so enforcement is not uniform. Consumers have already picked different copies: optimize.feasible_split (optimize.py:720-746) routes on the binding string 'regardless of the feasible boolean'. optimize.ConfigResult (98-177, no __post_init__) copies five of these fields a third time, each documented '== solution.X'. binding is a status string that is really an enum (heuristic 12), validated against the tuple _BINDING_VALUES (367-371).
findings.proposal: Without breaking the frozen surface, enforce in __post_init__ that feasible == (binding != 'infeasible_above_retail') and that the three representative copies equal outlay.representative's fields, with messages naming both values. This changes the behaviour of a frozen class's constructor, so it should be noted in the release. Turn ConfigResult's copies (not frozen) into properties over solution. Making binding an Enum or dropping the duplicated fields is a BREAKING change that needs a version bump. This spans finance and optimize.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — CostRecoverySolution.__post_init__ still checks only binding membership and the rate range, while its docstring states three 'Invariant:' lines. optimize.feasible_split still routes on the binding string, and ConfigResult still copies five fields with no __post_init__.

findings.statement: Heuristic 3, orthogonal dimensions of variability. The grid-services pricing axis (flat vs capacity-at-events) is a str field, grid_services_model (finance.py:114), with no single mechanism behind it. Four sites check it: FinanceConfig.__post_init__ validates the string against a local frozenset (178-183); project_multi_year has a fail-fast guard (1539-1544); _simulate_age branches on it (1601-1616), computing flat income inline there and event income in gridservices; and cli/finance.py:190-195 computes its own event figure from its own age-0 sim. The axis's invariant, capacity_at_events ⇒ grid_services_events is not None, is not enforced where the value is built (heuristic 10). The field docstring admits this: 'May be None even for that model (α only validates the selector field; γ/δ consume it)' (93-94). Measured: FinanceConfig(standing_charge_pence_per_day=60, grid_services_model='capacity_at_events') constructs. That inconsistent config then raises ConfigurationError in project_multi_year but silently renders no grid-services section in the CLI's report path, so the two call paths disagree on one invariant. The selector is a meaningful string, not a typed value (heuristic 12).
findings.proposal: Give the axis one mechanism: a small grid-services model value, flat(rate_per_kw) or events(GridServicesEventsConfig), with one method annual_income_gbp(fleet_results, homes, age). project_multi_year and the CLI call that method, and the per-age SOH fix for the known gap lives inside it. Enforce the events ⇒ config invariant in FinanceConfig.__post_init__. That changes construction behaviour of a frozen class, and replacing the str field's type is a BREAKING change needing a version bump. This spans finance, gridservices and cli.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — The grid_services_model str selector is still checked or branched at four sites: FinanceConfig.__post_init__, the project_multi_year guard, _simulate_age, and cli/finance.run L190-195. The field docstring still says 'α only validates the selector field'.

findings.statement: Heuristic 1, informative names. YearPoint.fleet_self_consumption_kwh (finance.py:1019) holds different things on its two producers. On project_multi_year's path it is the fleet's billed own-use: basis C, demand − import, or the capped override own-use. On spreadsheet_revenue_curve's path it is fraction × generation. A 22-line docstring note (1022-1041) explains that the name should be read as 'fleet billed own-use kWh'. That is the comment escalation the Comments stance names as a clarity symptom. The name points at exactly the quantity the briefing forbids substituting: the Basis-C convention says not to 'fix' own-use to physics self-consumption. Yet solve_cost_recovery_rate uses this field as its rate base (2303), and _NodeData.fleet_sc (1353) repeats the misnomer. A second smaller lie: fleet_revenue_gbp's docstring (1050) says it 'may have any sign', but its only physics producer clamps it at max(0.0, ...) (1779). YearPoint is outside the frozen surface: it is not in solar_challenge.__all__ and not in FROZEN_SURFACE or FROZEN_CLOSURE in test_public_api_surface.py. The field has no src consumer outside finance.py and 37 test references.
findings.proposal: Rename the field to fleet_billed_own_use_kwh (and _NodeData.fleet_sc to fleet_own_use) and delete the 22-line apology. Because YearPoint is outside the frozen contract, this is not a frozen-surface break, but the platform may import it from solar_challenge.finance, so the release notes should mention it. Also correct the 'any sign' docstring or drop the dead clamp. This is a mechanical rename within finance.py and its tests.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — YearPoint.fleet_self_consumption_kwh still carries the 22-line 'read it as billed own-use' note. solve_cost_recovery_rate.surplus_at still uses it as the rate base. project_multi_year still clamps fleet_revenue_gbp with max(0.0, ...) while the field docstring says 'may have any sign'.

findings.statement: Known gap (briefing finance-economics known_gaps[0], tracking: null), confirmed. Under grid_services_model='capacity_at_events', project_multi_year computes compute_grid_services_at_events once, from the first _simulate_age call (age 0, battery SOH reset to 1.0 by _aged_homes). It stores the result in _event_gs_memo (finance.py:1554, 1605-1610) and books that figure as CBS revenue in every sampled age and every one of the 25 interpolated years, so firm spare capacity never falls as SOH fades. tests/integration/test_grid_services_events.py::test_compute_once_event_figure_reused_across_ages (lines 240-280) asserts call_count == 1, so the suite enforces the gap. It does this by monkeypatching gridservices.compute_grid_services_at_events and relying on project_multi_year's function-local import. Doc-to-code gate: docs/cost-recovery-finance-model.md gives only the flat formula for grid_services_income (§4 lines 301-303, §8.1 lines 711-717, Summary table) and never mentions capacity_at_events, the memo, the event windows or the aggregator share. This branch changes fleet_revenue_gbp, and so the solved rate and the householder outlay, but has no equation in the board model doc, which breaks the convention that the doc has no unmodelled term. Two related drifts: GridServicesAtEvents' docstring (gridservices.py:476) calls the income 'householder-side' while project_multi_year books it as CBS revenue; and compute_fleet_spare_capacity_kw silently returns 0 kW for a window the simulated period does not cover (gridservices.py:455-456), so a summer-only window yields £0 with no warning.
findings.proposal: Pick between the PRD's two Open-Q1 options: compute spare capacity from each sampled age's own FleetResults, or scale E_spare by the per-age mean battery SOH. Either way, record the choice and its equations in a new capacity-at-events subsection of the model doc's §4 and §8.1, with a worked figure. Replace the call-count test with a behaviour test that income at the last seed age is at most the age-0 income on a fading fleet. Warn when no event window intersects the simulated period. This changes board numbers and spans finance, gridservices and the doc.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — _event_gs_memo still caches the age-0 compute_grid_services_at_events figure for every age and trial, behind a function-local import. The test still asserts call_count == 1 (test_grid_services_events.py:278). GridServicesAtEvents' docstring still says 'householder-side'.

findings.statement: Heuristic 13, files make internal sense in isolation. This is the 'function-local import placed to break a cycle' symptom. config.py:23 and :25 import finance.FinanceConfig and gridservices.EventWindow/GridServicesEventsConfig at top level, while both modules raise config.ConfigurationError. They reach it only through function-local imports. EventWindow.__post_init__ (gridservices.py:220-269) has eight per-branch imports. GridServicesEventsConfig.__post_init__ (345) has one. FinanceConfig.__post_init__ (finance.py:119, '# lazy: avoids import cycle') and project_multi_year (finance.py:1540) have two more. The workaround breaks heuristic 10's uniformity: GridServicesRateBand (gridservices.py:79-103) and flex.FlexibilityValueBand raise ValueError rather than ConfigurationError 'because ... importing ConfigurationError ... would re-introduce the import cycle'. One config tree therefore raises two unrelated exception types (ConfigurationError subclasses Exception, not ValueError; config.py:35). About 40 docstring lines defend the workaround (gridservices.py:35-40, 79-92, 223-234, 337-344). The workaround also inflates EventWindow.__post_init__ to cyclomatic 15 (radon C).
findings.proposal: Move ConfigurationError to a leaf module, for example solar_challenge/errors.py with no package imports. config, finance and gridservices import it at top level; config keeps using it, so solar_challenge.config.ConfigurationError still resolves without a pure shim. ConfigurationError is not in __all__. Then raise ConfigurationError uniformly from the rate-band and event-window validators, and delete the defensive prose. This spans modules.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — EventWindow.__post_init__ still has eight per-branch `from solar_challenge.config import ConfigurationError` imports, and GridServicesEventsConfig has one. The import graph marks all nine, plus finance.py:119 and :1540, as cycle-closing. GridServicesRateBand and FlexibilityValueBand still raise ValueError.

findings.statement: Heuristic 11, SPOT, and heuristic 9, narrow interfaces. Per config, _evaluate_config (optimize.py:937-1003) calls solve_cost_recovery_rate, which runs project_multi_year(scenario, finance) and one age-0 fleet sim. It then runs project_multi_year(scenario, finance) again with identical arguments (983) and a second age-0 fleet sim through _age0_baseline_outlay (865-916). solve_cost_recovery_rate does not surface its base curve or its age-0 summaries, so each config costs 8-26 fleet sims where 4-13 would do. The two age-0 fleets are also defined differently. finance builds its age-0 fleet as _aged_homes(homes, 0) plus _reconcile_seg_homes. _age0_baseline_outlay resets only PV age and skips SEG reconciliation. Measured with a capturing simulate on a home whose battery has system_age_years=6 and a scenario SEG of 4.1 p: the solve's age-0 fleet has battery soh=1.0 and seg_tariff=4.1 p, while _age0_baseline_outlay's has soh=None (so Battery derives 0.88 calendar SOH) and seg_tariff=None. So baseline_outlay_gbp, one Pareto axis, comes from a different fleet than baseline_surplus_per_home_gbp, the other axis, and from a different fleet than the solve's outlay. run_sweep's docstring (1051-1060) misstates all this: it says the solve runs project_multi_year 'at the solved rate' (it runs at the configured r0) and counts 'up to three' fleet simulations. The rate literal '15 p/kWh' appears 12 times in optimize.py, and output.py's '## Fixed-15p Trade-Off' header repeats it, although the value is finance.own_use_rate_pence_per_kwh. optimize also imports finance's private _resolve_homes (optimize.py:35).
findings.proposal: Have the solve's result carry, or a sibling public function return, the base MultiYearCurve and the age-0 SummaryStatistics. _evaluate_config would then reuse them and price the baseline outlay with bill_distribution at r0, so there is no second projection and no second age-0 definition. If the frozen CostRecoverySolution must not grow fields, add a non-exported finance function that returns (solution, base_curve, age0_summaries). Fix run_sweep's docstring and replace the '15p' literals with the configured rate. This spans finance, optimize and output.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — _evaluate_config still calls solve_cost_recovery_rate, then project_multi_year again with identical arguments, then _age0_baseline_outlay. run_sweep's docstring still says the solve runs project_multi_year 'at the solved rate' and counts 'up to three' simulations. grep counts 12 '15 p/kWh|15p' literals in optimize.py.

findings.statement: Heuristic 11, SPOT. A home's SEG rate has one home, HomeConfig.seg_tariff, which _reconcile_seg_homes fills from the scenario rate. On the override path, _seg_export_income_gbp (finance.py:650-695) re-derives that rate as physics export revenue ÷ physics export kWh and falls back to 0 when physics export is 0 (689-694). The override's export is then valued at £0 although a SEG tariff is configured. Measured: with override 0.7, generation 4,000 kWh and demand 3,400 kWh, the override exports 1,200 kWh. That earns £0.00 when physics export was 0 kWh, and £49.20 at 4.1 p when physics export was 1 kWh. A zero-export window is plausible for the short winter windows the model doc's §7.6 describes. householder_bill's sibling re-derivation of the import rate (955-960) falls back to retail instead, so the two ratio reconstructions disagree on what an empty denominator means. No path values export at the import rate, so the briefing's export convention holds. The doc (§4 line 289) documents the zero fallback.
findings.proposal: Pass the home's SEG rate as a structured value: carry seg_tariff, or its rate, on the per-home record the projection reads, and price override export at that rate rather than reconstructing it from a ratio. Update the doc's §4 override line. The change is local to finance.py and the doc, and it changes CBS revenue only on zero-export windows.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — _seg_export_income_gbp still re-derives the SEG rate as export_rev_physics / export_kwh and falls back to 0.0 when physics export is 0.

findings.statement: Heuristic 11, SPOT, applied to the bill identities. bill() (finance.py:751-864) is the arithmetic single source of truth: householder_bill (872-975) only resolves inputs and duplicates no arithmetic, and no bill arithmetic exists outside finance.py. VAT is applied once, to import + standing + own-use. But the identity list has three prose homes, and they have drifted. BillBreakdown's docstring (199-209, 233, 250, 268-279) describes annual figures ('Annual grid standing charge', 'Total annual householder outlay'). It also gives self_consumption_saving = sc × (retail − own_use) and a baseline at the retail rate. bill() is period-native and uses eff_rate = baseline_import_cost/demand. Measured: bill(period_days=30, ...) returns standing_charge_gbp=18.0, not an annual figure. With a 50 £ baseline on 280 kWh, self_consumption_saving_gbp is 3.0, where BillBreakdown's documented formula gives 8.4. The model doc traces VAT, outlay and saving to householder_bill() (§3 line 112; Summary table lines 796-803) and never names bill(), so a reviewer following the doc-to-code gate lands on a function with no VAT arithmetic. Separately, the same Summary table's capex row (806) drops the inverter term that §6 and project_economics both carry.
findings.proposal: Keep the identity list only in bill()'s docstring. Make BillBreakdown's field docstrings say 'for the billed period' and point to bill(). Point the model doc's §3 and Summary rows at bill() as the arithmetic and householder_bill() as the annual wrapper, and add the inverter term to the Summary capex row. These are documentation-only changes in one module and one doc.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — BillBreakdown's docstring still describes annual figures and self_consumption_saving at the retail rate. bill() is still period-native and uses eff_rate = baseline_import_cost / demand.

findings.statement: The solve's docstring (finance.py:2211-2215) and the model doc's §5 (lines 387, 403-404) say that net surplus is 'exactly affine' in r because 'PCHIP interpolation is a linear operator on node values'. That is false: scipy's PchipInterpolator takes weighted harmonic means of the secant slopes at interior nodes and clips the end slopes, so it is non-linear in the node values. surplus_at(r) (2297-2310) is affine only because it shifts the already-interpolated revenue curve by (r-r0)/100 × the separately interpolated own-use curve, and that is not the curve project_multi_year would produce at rate r. Measured with finance._interpolate_per_year on plausible node shapes (scratch scripts pchip_affine2.py and r0dep.py): per-year fleet revenue differs by up to £41-150 a year from a re-interpolation at r. Mean surplus per home is exact on equal-width node sets (seeds 0/12/24), but after bisection adds an unequal node it is off by £0.001-0.11/home/yr. The solved rate then depends on the configured own_use_rate_pence_per_kwh (r0), an input the doc treats as irrelevant: r* spreads by 0.004-0.010 p/kWh across r0 ∈ {0, 15, 23}. This excludes any r0 effect on which bisection nodes are picked, since revenue deviation drives that. The doc's worked examples use a flat curve, so they still reproduce to the penny. Real board runs are not exactly closed-form.
findings.proposal: Either correct the claim in the docstring and doc §5: affine by construction of the reconstruction, exact at the nodes, with a stated bound. Or make it exact: have _NodeData carry the rate-independent revenue C separately and build per-year revenue as PCHIP(C) + r/100·PCHIP(own-use), so the solve is affine in r and independent of r0. The second option changes the projection's revenue curve slightly and chooses a design.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — The solve docstring still says net surplus is 'exactly affine' because 'PCHIP interpolation is a linear operator on node values'. _interpolate_per_year still uses scipy PchipInterpolator, which is non-linear.

findings.statement: Heuristic 11, SPOT. Two coexisting grid-services band tables use the same low/central/high labels with no derivation linking them. flex.FLEX_VALUE_BANDS (flex.py:114-139) gives a flat 1.5, 12 and 48 £ per kW of max discharge per year. gridservices.GRID_SERVICES_RATE_BANDS (gridservices.py:152-168) gives 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 £/kW/event plus 30, 60 and 120 £/MWh. Only a comment ties them: central '£12/kW/yr ≈ £1/kW/event for ~12 events/yr' (143-146). Measured with the defaults (DEFAULT_EVENT_WINDOWS, utilisation 0.6, aggregator 25%), the event bands net 4.99, 9.97 and 19.94 £ per kW of firm spare capacity per year. Because spare capacity ≤ max discharge, 'high' is under half of flat high, the band spread is 4× where flat's is 32×, and only central lines up. The band vocabulary itself is defined four times: the flex dict keys, the GridServicesRateBands fields plus the if-chain in resolve() (120-140), GridServicesEventsConfig's own _VALID_BANDS frozenset (347, a second validator that does not call resolve), and cli/finance.py:53's FlexBand enum. FLEX_VALUE_BANDS is a mutable module-level dict while its sibling is frozen (heuristic 8). flex.py:96's pointer 'config.py:264 default' is stale: the 2.5 kW default is battery.py:162. Both band tables are labelled provisional (open-Q2).
findings.proposal: Define the band vocabulary once, as an Enum or Literal in one module that both tables key on. Validate through that one resolver. Freeze FLEX_VALUE_BANDS with MappingProxyType. Either derive the events-model defaults from the flat bands with a stated events-per-year factor, or document in the model doc that the two models' bands are independent calibrations. Changing GridServicesEventsConfig.band's type would be a BREAKING change. This spans flex, gridservices and cli.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — FLEX_VALUE_BANDS is still a mutable dict and GRID_SERVICES_RATE_BANDS is still frozen and unlinked to it. The resolve() if-chain and GridServicesEventsConfig's _VALID_BANDS are unchanged. Additional evidence: cli/optimize._SENSITIVITY_ALIAS_MAP['grid_services'] restates the flat per-kW values (1.5, 12.0, 48.0) as literals, a third copy. flex.resolve_grid_services_band has 0 src callers.

findings.statement: Tests stance. tests/integration/test_optimize_sweep.py:35-37 imports _pareto_baseline, _rank_feasible and _split_infeasible, and tests/integration/test_optimize_sensitivity.py imports _build_axis_configs (9 call sites). The first three (optimize.py:919-934) have zero callers in src: run_sweep calls the public feasible_split, rank and pareto_baseline directly (1082-1089). They are pure one-line delegators kept only so the tests resolve, which is heuristic 13's shim symptom, and run_sweep's docstring (1027) still sends readers to _rank_feasible. _build_axis_configs is reached because sensitivity_panel exposes no seam for 'one knob applied to the configs'. No test patches an optimize private name.
findings.proposal: Retarget the sweep tests to the public rank, feasible_split and pareto_baseline, delete the three delegators, and fix run_sweep's docstring. Either make knob application public (apply_knob) or test it through sensitivity_panel with an injected simulate. Mechanical and local.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — _split_infeasible, _rank_feasible and _pareto_baseline are still pure delegators with 0 src callers (grep). Tests still reach them: 13 _pareto_baseline, 10 _rank_feasible, 5 _split_infeasible and 12 _build_axis_configs occurrences. run_sweep's docstring still points at _rank_feasible.

findings.statement: Heuristic 2, simple control flows. sensitivity_panel (optimize.py:506-639) scores 26 cognitive (complexipy) and 14 cyclomatic (radon C). Most of the branching exists because the retained-cash floor has two setters: a FinanceConfig field reachable through _build_axis_configs, and run_sweep's retained_cash_floor_gbp override, which would clobber it. The loop therefore special-cases the floor axis by its literal name (598-606), short-circuits it against the panel floor (600-601), and keeps a (name, value) cache (582-614). _build_axis_configs (440-503, cognitive 13) routes knob names through three string-matched branches (heuristic 3 and heuristic 12 in miniature).
findings.proposal: Give the floor one setter: either run_sweep stops overriding the floor and the panel applies it through _build_axis_configs like any other FinanceConfig knob, or the reverse. The floor special case and its short-circuit then go away. This is local to optimize, with one design choice.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — sensitivity_panel still special-cases the floor axis by its literal name, short-circuits on `v == retained_cash_floor_gbp` and keeps a (name, value) cache. Snapshot cognitive is 26. Finding finance-economics.5 adds that the short-circuit never fires on the CLI default path.

findings.statement: api.py::simulate_sweep re-derives SweepSpec's validation and get_values inline. min, max and steps are read with bare float()/int(), so an infinite value is an OverflowError and a 500 (live task 440). Any mode string other than 'geometric' silently runs linear, whereas SweepSpec.__post_init__ refuses an unknown mode. steps has only a lower bound: steps=10**6 parses 10**6 HomeConfigs and submits 10**6 jobs (live task 140 asks for a Steps max). parameter-sweep.js previewValues is a third copy of the point generation. Its parameterOptions restate ranges that disagree with the server: PV 1-20 against parse_home_config's 0.5-20, consumption 1000-10000 against FLEET_COMPONENTS load 500-20000, and battery 0-50 against FLEET_COMPONENTS battery 0-100. The handler also has gratuitous function-local imports (uuid, math) that break no cycle.
findings.proposal: Add web/sweep_request.py::read_sweep_request(body) -> SweepRequest(parameter, home_key, spec: config.SweepSpec). It reads min and max with as_finite_float_within(parameter range), steps with as_whole_number_within(2, MAX_SWEEP_POINTS), and mode against a Literal['linear','geometric'] passed explicitly. It then constructs SweepSpec and uses spec.get_values(). One _SWEEP_PARAMETERS table (key, home key, range taken from FLEET_COMPONENTS and the home PV bound) is rendered to the page, and the page renders its options from it. What becomes deletable: the inline validation and math in simulate_sweep, the hard-coded parameterOptions, and _SWEEP_PARAMETER_HOME_KEYS as a separate table. This would have prevented 440, 140 and 128 (unsupported parameters).
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — Read api.py::simulate_sweep at 7dfea36. min, max and steps go through bare float()/int() (541-543), only steps < 2 is refused (546), any mode other than 'geometric' runs linear (554-563), and the function-local imports of uuid (530) and math (555) are still there. parameter-sweep.js still defines previewValues (line 27).

findings.statement: There is one producer and two consumers of the progress stream, and no shared definition of what the stream says. In api.py::_job_event_payload each event type gets a different subset of JobState, in a different key order: progress has 4 keys, complete has 5 and error has 2. api.py::get_job_progress also writes three frames by hand, outside that builder: the 10-minute timeout and 'Job not found' frames as {"error": ...}, and, for a subscriber that arrives after another stream drained the queue, a complete frame with only status and run_id (live task 641). So the same event name 'error' carries two payload shapes, {status, message} and {error}. Each consumer reconciles them with its own fallbacks: progress-tracker.js uses `data.message || data.error`, and parameter-sweep.js uses a try/catch around JSON.parse. Naming the server event 'error' also collides with the native EventSource 'error' event that fires on a dropped connection. Both consumers add one listener for both, and progress-tracker.js::_onError and parameter-sweep.js::_followPoint then mark a still-running job 'failed' when the connection drops (live task 648). The sweep page likewise marks a point failed when the server's timeout frame arrives (live task 564). In addition, JobEvent.type is fully determined by JobState.status (running→progress, completed→complete, failed→error), so one fact is stored twice; the late-subscriber branch re-derives it inline, and the post-pin amend _FINAL_EVENT_TYPE_BY_STATUS re-derives it a third time.
findings.proposal: Define the stream once as a typed frame. JobFrame is the full asdict(JobState), with the same keys on every frame, and the event name is computed from status by one mapping, e.g. JOB_STREAM_EVENT[status] -> 'job-progress' | 'job-complete' | 'job-failed', named so it cannot collide with EventSource's 'error'. Stream-level endings (timeout, unknown job) become a distinct 'stream-closed' event whose `reason` is a Literal. Delete JobEvent.type, which is derivable, along with _job_event_payload's per-type branches and the three inline frames in get_job_progress. On the client, one module (static/js/job-stream.js: jobStream(jobId, {onState, onEnd, onDisconnected})) is the only parser, used by both progress-tracker.js and parameter-sweep.js. A transport drop then goes to onDisconnected, which keeps the last state and lets EventSource reconnect. Pin the contract with a test that asserts the frame keys equal JobState's fields. This would have prevented 641 (a late frame with different fields), 648 (a drop read as a failure), 564 (a timeout read as a failure on the sweep page), and the 533/638/649 rework that each changed one consumer.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — Read api.py:155-240. _job_event_payload still sends 4, 5 and 2 keys per type. The hand-written frames remain: timeout {error} at 203, 'Job not found' {error} at 208, and the two-field complete at 220-223. progress-tracker.js:61 still reads data.message || data.error, and both JS consumers addEventListener('error') (progress-tracker.js:23, parameter-sweep.js:165).

findings.statement: A job's progress through queued→running→completed|failed is recorded as four separate facts with no legal-transition table: JobState.status, _TrackedJob.finished_at, the jobs-row status and the runs-row status. JobManager._report_state overwrites the state with whatever it is handed. Only _run_job's try/except makes a job terminal, and the executor boundary does not: JobManager._finish_job, the done-callback that runs however the future ends, stamps finished_at without checking that status is terminal. Every path that leaves _run_job's try therefore leaves a job that is finished but still 'queued' or 'running' in memory and in both rows. That covers sqlite3.connect or the PRAGMA failing before the try (live task 646), _record_failed_job's own _state_of_running_job raising inside the except, and a queued future cancelled by shutdown(cancel_futures=True). An SSE stream on that job then heartbeats until its 10-minute cap, and the job silently ages out after _FINISHED_JOB_TTL_SECONDS. Run status also has two writers that can reverse each other. RunStorage.save_home_run/save_fleet_run upsert the run as 'completed' inside work_fn. If the following _record_completed_job UPDATE raises (for example 'database is locked' with two workers), the except branch's _record_failed_run_row turns that completed run, whose files are on disk, into 'failed'. That completed→failed transition is illegal, and nothing refuses it.
findings.proposal: Introduce a JobLifecycle with a single writer, JobManager._transition(job_id, new_state). It checks LEGAL_JOB_TRANSITIONS = {queued: {running, failed}, running: {running, completed, failed}}. An illegal move raises an error naming the job, the old status and the new one, and terminal states are final. Make terminality a property of the executor boundary: _finish_job reads future.exception() / future.cancelled(), and if the tracked status is not terminal it transitions the job to failed, with the escaped exception or 'dropped by shutdown' as the message. With that in place _run_job's try/except no longer has to be exhaustive, and the 646 class cannot recur. Run status should follow the job: either RunStorage's save stops writing status and the lifecycle writes 'completed' after the save, or the lifecycle skips the failed write once the run is completed. The legality check also removes the completed→failed overwrite. recover_stale_jobs should be expressed through the same table (queued|running → failed).
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — Read jobs.py:482-495. _finish_job stamps finished_at without checking that the status is terminal. _run_job still opens sqlite3.connect and runs the PRAGMA before its try (598-600). _report_state overwrites the state unconditionally (545-553), and the save upsert writes 'completed' before _record_completed_job.

findings.statement: save_home_run writes summary_json from SummaryStatistics and save_fleet_run writes it from FleetSummary, and the two key sets differ. For example, FleetSummary has fleet_self_consumption_ratio and no self_consumption_ratio, grid_dependency_ratio or total_battery_charge_kwh. Yet RunRecord.decoded_summary returns Any, and the run's `type` never selects a schema on the way out. At least six readers read home keys by string. api.history_list_runs and assistant.list_recent_runs read summary.get('self_consumption_ratio'), which is None for every fleet run (live 653). charts.comparison_radar, reached from history.compare_page, reads self_consumption_ratio, grid_dependency_ratio and total_battery_charge_kwh with default 0, so fleets draw at 0% (live 565, 654). routes._get_aggregate_stats reads json_extract(summary_json,'$.total_generation_kwh'), which works for both types only because the two key sets happen to share that name. parameter-sweep.js reads s.self_consumption_ratio from api.get_job_results. There are also three decoders of the same text with different failure behaviour. RunRecord.decoded_summary swallows a decode error and returns {}. api.get_job_results calls json.loads and raises, giving a 500. assistant.get_run_results calls json.loads and the error is caught as a 'Database error'.
findings.proposal: Make the decoded summary typed and tagged by run type. RunRecord.summary() -> SummaryStatistics | FleetSummary | None dispatches on self.type through the existing _deserialize_dataclass. Add a frozen RunHeadline (generation_kwh, self_consumption_ratio, grid_import_kwh, battery_charge_kwh | None, ...) built by one function, run_headline(summary), which matches on the summary type. That function is the only place that knows fleet_self_consumption_ratio corresponds to self_consumption_ratio. History list, assistant list/get, aggregate stats, get_job_results (and so the sweep page) and the compare charts serialize RunHeadline and stop calling .get on raw keys. With every reader on it, the string-key reads and the json_extract key become deletable, as do the three ad-hoc json.loads paths. A missing headline field becomes a type error in one function rather than a null in four pages. This would have prevented 653, 565, 654 and the 410 rounding/summary drift.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — storage.py:195-197: decoded_summary -> Any, with no schema chosen by type. assistant.get_run_results:510 and api.get_job_results:270 still call json.loads raw. api.history_list_runs:697-703 and assistant.list_recent_runs:572-573 still read 'self_consumption_ratio' by string.

findings.statement: No production code reads the jobs table. A grep of src/ finds only jobs.py's own INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, and JobManager.job_state's docstring says the manager 'never reads the jobs table'. recover_stale_jobs only UPDATEs it and uses rowcount for a log line, while the runs rows are recovered by their own status. Even so, every transition writes it: one INSERT, an UPDATE plus commit on each progress tick (a fleet emits one per home), a second UPDATE just for started_at, the completed UPDATE, the failed UPDATE with error_traceback, which is never shown anywhere, and the DELETE in _forget_job. _run_job opens a sqlite3 connection before its try only to carry these writes. Neither runner's work_fn uses the `conn` it is passed, because RunStorage opens its own. That connection is the pre-try code of live task 646. So job state lives in two stores, one of them never read, and keeping them consistent produced a run of fixes and amends: 543 (track only after both rows are written), 627 (per-row transactions and logging), amends 06eaa8d, 45ea53f and 78c64c6, and 6e82f01 (_forget_job deletes the rows of a refused job).
findings.proposal: Pick one home for a job's state. The briefing already makes the in-memory JobManager authoritative for live jobs, and the runs row is the durable record of the outcome. Under that choice, delete the jobs-table writes: the jobs INSERT in _record_new_job, the UPDATEs in _update_progress, _run_job's started_at UPDATE, _record_completed_job's UPDATE, _record_failed_job_row, the jobs DELETE in _forget_job and the jobs UPDATE in recover_stale_jobs. Then delete _run_job's connection and work_fn's unused conn parameter, and drop the table (database.py has no migrations, so the table can simply stop being created). If a durable job record is actually wanted, for example so /api/jobs/<id> answers after the 1 h TTL, make job_state fall back to the table so it has a reader. Either way, every write gets a reader or is deleted.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — grep of src/ for FROM jobs / jobs WHERE outside jobs.py finds nothing. Neither work() closure uses conn (jobs.py:648-667, 702-734), each builds its own RunStorage (656, 723), and the progress UPDATE+commit runs on every tick (512-533).

findings.statement: RunStorage derives its runs upsert from RunRecord's fields (storage.py::_run_row_upsert, added by task 577 to stop the INSERT being restated). JobManager._record_new_job still restates the same 12-column INSERT positionally, with inline None comments. Run status has two writers: RunStorage's upsert writes 'completed', and jobs.py writes 'running' at insert, 'failed' in _record_failed_run_row and in recover_stale_jobs, and deletes in _forget_job. Reads also bypass RunStorage. api.history_list_runs builds its own WHERE/ORDER/LIMIT query, which duplicates RunStorage.list_runs' filtering with a different filter set. routes._get_aggregate_stats has a function-local get_db import and a literal status = 'completed'. assistant.list_recent_runs runs its own SELECT. Each of these restates the column set and the status vocabulary outside the RunStatus Literal's reach. One stated fact goes unenforced: RunType declares 'sweep', and runs.html offers a 'Sweep' filter, but no writer ever stores type 'sweep'. Sweep points are saved as 'home' runs named 'Sweep x=y', so that filter always returns nothing. JobManager also takes db_path/data_dir on every submit and builds a new RunStorage per job instead of using the app's one.
findings.proposal: Make RunStorage the only module that issues SQL against runs, and inject it into JobManager (JobManager(storage=...)) so submits stop carrying db_path/data_dir. Move the remaining operations into RunStorage: create_queued_run(id, name, type, n_homes, created_at), built from RunRecord like the upsert; mark_run_failed(id, message, at); forget_run(id); fail_interrupted_runs(); a page_runs(filter: RunQuery) that returns RunRecords plus a total, replacing both history_list_runs' SQL and list_runs; and aggregate_stats(). Status values come from RunStatus constants. Deletable: the INSERT in _record_new_job, _record_failed_run_row's SQL, the SQL in api.history_list_runs, routes._get_aggregate_stats and assistant.list_recent_runs, plus routes.py's function-local get_db import. Either write 'sweep' runs or delete 'sweep' from RunType and the filter option.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — jobs.py:427-450 still has the positional 12-column runs INSERT with inline None comments. routes._get_aggregate_stats:34-44 still has its local get_db import and the literal status = 'completed'. assistant.list_recent_runs:549-557 still runs its own SELECT.

findings.statement: Each _TrackedJob has one deque (maxlen=100) of JobEvents, and JobManager.get_events copies and clears it under the lock. Whichever caller drains first therefore consumes the events, even though the method's name says 'get' (live 680). A job's stream regularly has more than one subscriber: EventSource reconnects automatically, a second tab or a page reload opens a new stream, and the sweep page and the results page can follow the same job. The consumers need the latest state, not a log: every frame carries a full JobState snapshot, and progress is idempotent. Because a second subscriber finds the queue empty, api.get_job_progress needs a compensating branch that rebuilds a terminal frame from job_state, and that branch is where the 641 two-field complete frame came from. It also has to read job_state and drain events in two separate lock holds and reason about the race between them.
findings.proposal: Replace the event queue with a versioned snapshot. _TrackedJob keeps state plus a monotonically increasing version, bumped by _report_state, and the manager exposes a non-destructive job_snapshot(job_id) -> (version, JobState). Each stream keeps its own cursor and emits a frame whenever the version moves, ending when the snapshot's status is terminal. Deletable: _TrackedJob.events, JobEvent's queue role, get_events, and get_job_progress's late-subscriber terminal branch. Multiple subscribers, reconnects and late subscribers all get the same frames, which removes the bug class behind 641 and 680.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — jobs.py:360-380 still copies and clears the deque under the lock. api.get_job_progress:217-227 still has the compensating terminal branch.

findings.statement: Only the outer object has a shared rule at the boundary: shared.require_json_object, which task 249 introduced and which maps to 400 through the blueprint's NotAJsonObject handler. Fields are read ad hoc. api.simulate_fleet_api passes data.get('name') unchecked into JobManager.submit_fleet_job and on to the runs INSERT, so a non-string name raises sqlite3's ProgrammingError and answers 500 (live 517, together with parse_home_config's unchecked params['name']). api.simulate_sweep reads mode with str(data.get('mode')) and treats any value other than 'geometric', including a typo, as linear, although its docstring lists only 'linear' | 'geometric'. parse_home_config reads bool(params['stochastic']), so the string 'false' runs the stochastic model. shared.resolve_location turns an unrecognised location into Bristol. api.py has five per-endpoint `except (ValueError, TypeError) -> 400` blocks, each catching whatever its own coercions happen to raise. Under this structure each new field is another chance of a 500 or a silent default (14 mined fixes: 165, 243, 249/268, 435, 557, 339; live 331, 517, 560).
findings.proposal: Parse each request body once into a frozen request record (HomeRunRequest, FleetRunRequest, SweepRequest with mode: Literal['linear','geometric']) using one parse_request(cls, body) helper. The helper refuses wrong JSON types, unknown Literal values and over-long strings by raising a single RequestRefused(field, value, expected) error, and the api blueprint's errorhandler maps it to 400 as it already does for NotAJsonObject. JobManager.submit_* then take the typed record. Deletable: the five ad-hoc except blocks, the str()/bool()/float() coercions in simulate_sweep and parse_home_config, and the silent fallbacks. Recurrence of 517, 331 and 560 is then structurally ruled out.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — api.py:120 still passes data.get('name', 'Fleet Simulation') unchecked. simulation_params.py:342 still has bool(params['stochastic']) and :344 params['name']. simulate_sweep:550 still has str(data.get('mode')).

findings.statement: shared.py::resolve_location maps a preset name or a 'lat,lon' string to a Location. For anything else, such as 'Paris', 'lodnon' or '51.5;-0.1', it catches ValueError and returns Location.bristol(). The same happens to an out-of-range 'lat,lon', because Location's own ValueError is caught too. The simulation then runs, and is saved and reported, for Bristol while the request named somewhere else, with no 400 and no warning. The assistant's run_home_simulation tool passes model-written location strings through the same path, so a model's typo produces a plausible-looking result for the wrong place. The function's name says it resolves the location it is given, which it does not do in this case.
findings.proposal: Raise a ValueError that names the value and the accepted forms (the LOCATION_PRESETS keys, or 'lat,lon'), and let it propagate. parse_home_config's callers already answer ValueError with 400, and the assistant tools already turn it into an {error} dict. Delete the Bristol fallback.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — shared.py:59-72 (file lines) still catches ValueError and returns Location.bristol().

findings.statement: chat() breaks the chat_messages invariant it exists to keep (one assistant row with real content after every user row) on two paths. (1) An API error before the first streamed token (rate limit after retries, 529 overload, a bad key or SOLAR_ASSISTANT_MODEL, a network fault) lands in the except at assistant.py:1012-1022, which saves an assistant row whose content is the empty accumulated text. The next request replays it as a non-final message (assistant.py:879-883). Probe: a fake client whose first stream raises before any delta, then a normal second turn; the second call was sent [{'role':'user','content':'hello'},{'role':'assistant','content':''},{'role':'user','content':'again'}]. The Messages API refuses empty content on any message but an optional final assistant message, so every later turn in that browser session 400s, and each 400 runs the same except and appends another empty row; nothing in the assistant blueprint or assistant.js starts a new conversation, and the session cookie is not permanent, so this lasts until the browser session ends. The API refusal itself could not be exercised offline; the replayed request is confirmed. (2) A client disconnect mid-reply raises GeneratorExit at a yield. It is a BaseException, so neither the except (1012) nor the success save (1028) runs. Probe: read the first delta frame, close the response; /assistant/history then holds only the user row, and the reply the user saw is lost, together with any run_home_simulation/run_fleet_simulation job the turn submitted. The rationale comment at 1013-1016 says a dangling user row is what the API rejects with a 400; the claude-api reference says consecutive same-role turns are combined, so the comment defends the shape that is harmless and hides the one that is not.
findings.proposal: Give the assistant turn one persistence point that runs on every exit (try/finally around the loop, GeneratorExit included). It must never persist empty content: either store a non-empty placeholder (e.g. the error notice the user was shown) or skip the row and drop the dangling user turn from the replayed window. The replay window should also skip empty assistant rows already in existing databases. Pin both paths with tests: an error before the first token followed by a second turn, and a disconnect after the first frame. Replace the stale comment with a pointer to that test. This choice stays inside assistant.py.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — assistant.py:1012-1022 still saves `accumulated` (possibly '') as the assistant row with no emptiness check, and nothing handles GeneratorExit. More evidence: the success path at 1028-1030 also saves `accumulated` unchecked. A final message whose stop_reason is not tool_use and which streamed no text (e.g. a refusal) therefore stores an empty assistant row too.

findings.statement: The progress stream gives up after 10 minutes of its own lifetime (max_duration = 600, api.py:200-204). It ends with the same 'event: error' that a failed job sends, with data {"error": "SSE stream timed out after 10 minutes"}. progress-tracker.js:55-65 reads any error frame with data as the job's failure: it sets status 'failed', shows the message, and closes the stream. The job keeps running and later completes, and the page never learns. The cap is reachable by ordinary use. A fleet job simulates its homes one after another in one worker thread (jobs.py:707-713), and a 30-day single-home run took 3.5 s here on synthetic weather, so a full-year home is about 40 s. A full-year 100-home fleet, the canonical Bristol shape, is therefore about 70 minutes. The fleet-from-distribution form accepts up to MAX_FLEET_HOMES = 10,000 homes (fleet_config.py:32). The 'Job not found' branch reuses the same event too, so 'the stream stopped' and 'the job failed' cannot be told apart by event type (heuristic 12). complexipy scores the generator's route at 22. No test pins the cap.
findings.proposal: Do not report a stream limit as a job outcome. On reaching the cap, end the response without an error frame and let EventSource reconnect, which resumes from the job's current state because each loop reads job_state afresh; or drop the cap and rely on the heartbeat writes to detect a gone client. Give 'job unknown' its own event type if the page must treat it differently. Add a test with a fake clock. The change is mechanical and stays in api.py.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — api.py:199-204: max_duration = 600 still ends the stream with event: error {error}, which progress-tracker.js:55-65 reads as failure.

findings.statement: Deleting a run whose job is still queued or running does not delete it. history_delete_run (api.py:747-762) checks only that the row exists, then RunStorage.delete_run (storage.py:745-766) deletes the runs row, which cascades to the jobs row (database.py:91 ON DELETE CASCADE, foreign_keys ON in get_db and in _run_job), and removes the directory. The worker carries on. Its progress UPDATEs hit zero rows without complaint (jobs.py:512-533). Then save_home_run or save_fleet_run writes the files again and _upsert_run_row (storage.py:360-368) INSERTs the row again, because no row is left to conflict with. Probe: a gated simulate_home, POST /api/simulate/home, DELETE /api/history/runs/<id> (200, then GET 404), release the gate. GET then answers 200 with status 'completed' and the original name, and the job reports completed. The upsert that keeps a rename made while the job runs (_COLUMNS_A_RESAVE_KEEPS, storage.py:225, pinned by test_web_jobs.py:960) is the same statement that brings a deleted run back. Concurrent label edits were designed for; concurrent deletion was not. The Run History table offers Delete on every row, running ones included (templates/history/runs.html:215-224).
findings.proposal: Choose one contract. (a) Refuse to delete an unfinished run: answer 409 while the run's status is 'running', which RunRecord already exposes, and hide the button for such rows. (b) Make deletion win: the job's final save becomes an UPDATE that writes nothing when the row is gone, and the files are written only if the row still exists. (a) is one check at the API boundary. (b) changes the save contract shared by jobs.py and storage.py. Pin the chosen one with a test.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — api.py:747-762 still checks only that the row exists. storage.delete_run:745-766 still deletes the row and the dir. The upsert at storage.py:360-368 can still re-INSERT the row, and nothing refuses deleting a run whose status is 'running'.

findings.statement: Heuristic 12 (parse at the boundary into typed values): several /api endpoints pass request values to SQLite or to str methods without reading their type. A wrong type then answers 500 instead of 400, and the 500 is the app's HTML error page (app.py:144-146), because api_bp registers a JSON handler only for NotAJsonObject (api.py:56-62). Probes (TESTING off): POST /api/simulate/fleet with name {'x': 1} gives 500 (fleet_name = data.get('name', ...) at api.py:120 reaches the runs INSERT); POST /api/presets with name 5 gives 500 (data.get('name', '').strip(), api.py:321); PATCH /api/history/runs/<id> with name {'a': 1} gives 500 text/html (labels go to update_run_labels unread, api.py:783); POST /api/simulate/home with name ['a'] gives 500 (parse_home_config returns params['name'] unread, simulation_params.py:344). Elsewhere numbers are coerced loosely rather than read: simulate_sweep's int(data.get('steps')) truncates 2.9 to 2 and accepts true as 1 (api.py:543).
findings.proposal: Read each endpoint's labels and names with one shared typed reader (a str-or-absent rule like require_json_object's, raising a refusal that api_bp maps to 400), including parse_home_config's name. Give api_bp a JSON 500 handler so JSON clients never receive the HTML error page. This spans api.py and simulation_params.py and changes no frozen surface.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — api.py:321 data.get('name', '').strip() is unchanged, as are api.py:783 (labels passed unread to update_run_labels) and api.py:543 int(data.get('steps')). api_bp still registers only the NotAJsonObject handler (56-62).

findings.statement: The assistant's 'grounded' benchmark facts (the comment at assistant.py:~78-82 says explain_metric answers from this table 'so the model quotes these benchmark numbers instead of hallucinating them') contradict each other and the engine's own single sources. Ofgem TDCV appears three ways in one file: the system prompt says low 2,900 / medium 3,100 / high 4,200 (assistant.py:62); annual_consumption says 1,900 / 2,900 / 4,200 (:162); grid_import says 1,900 / 2,700 / 4,100 (:127). The engine's table is load.OFGEM_TDCV_BY_OCCUPANTS (load.py:24-30). PV-only self-consumption is '30-40 %' and with a battery '55-70 %' (assistant.py:93-94), while validation.py judges runs against 20-45 % and 50-90 % (validation.py:364-366, 444-445) and its docstrings say 25-35 % / 60-80 %. Bristol yield is 'typically 900-970 kWh/kWp' (assistant.py:172) and suggest_config sizes PV at _UK_YIELD_KWH_PER_KWP = 950 (:216), while the engine's measured Bristol yield is ~1000 kWh/kWp (docs/pv-system-losses.md:81-82, PVGIS 1001-1023). So the assistant tells a user the engine's default result is above typical for Bristol, and undersizes PV relative to the model it then runs.
findings.proposal: Have METRIC_TABLE and the system prompt read the engine's constants: load.OFGEM_TDCV_BY_OCCUPANTS, and validation's self-consumption and yield bands, once those are hoisted to named module constants (they are inline literals now). Have suggest_config derive yield from the documented model figure. Delete the duplicated prose numbers. This spans web, load and validation; no frozen names change.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — The three TDCV versions remain: the system prompt 2,900/3,100/4,200 (62), grid_import 1,900/2,700/4,100 (127-128) and annual_consumption 1,900/2,900/4,200 (161-162). The 30-40 %/55-70 % bands (93-94), 900-970 kWh/kWp (172) and _UK_YIELD_KWH_PER_KWP = 950.0 (216) are unchanged.

findings.statement: Heuristic 4 (small function scopes) and heuristic 2 (simple control flows): chat() spans assistant.py:824-1034, about 210 lines. complexipy scores it 47, against the doc's Sonar threshold of 15; it is the highest of the six web server modules (get_job_progress is next at 22, simulate_sweep at 17). One nested generator holds the API-key and empty-message prechecks, client construction, saving the user turn, history windowing with role repair, run-context injection, request assembly, the bounded agentic loop with tool dispatch and SSE framing, the cap notice, and two more persistence sites. Persistence is split across three save_chat_message calls (874, 1017, 1028) with different metadata shapes. Heuristic 6 (well-defined purpose): the function's purpose cannot be stated without several 'and's. The Comments stance: about 25 inline comment lines explain the loop's invariants, and one of them (1013-1016) is already wrong (see the kind:defect finding at this anchor). The persistence defects sit exactly where this structure scatters the turn's lifecycle.
findings.proposal: Split chat() into named steps with stateless interfaces: a function that builds the request messages from stored history and an optional run context (pure, testable without Flask); a function that runs the tool loop and yields typed events (delta, tool, cap, done, error); a single turn-recorder that persists the outcome once; and the route, which only frames events as SSE. Move the loop's invariants into tests and drop the inline commentary. The work stays within assistant.py.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — chat() still spans assistant.py:824-1034 as one nested generator with three save_chat_message sites (874, 1017, 1028).

findings.statement: Every web route that takes a location, and the assistant's trigger tools, run Bristol silently when the location is unrecognised or invalid. resolve_location (web/shared.py:59-72) catches ValueError and returns Location.bristol(), and the ValueError it swallows includes Location's own range refusal. Probe: resolve_location('cardiff'), resolve_location('95,0') and parse_home_config({'pv_kw': 4, 'location': 'cardiff', 'days': 1}) all yield 'Bristol, UK'. It is called from simulation_params.parse_home_config (:354), which serves POST /api/simulate/home and /simulate/fleet, the sweep and both assistant tools, and from web/fleet_scenario.py:131. Every other field parse_home_config reads is refused naming the field and value, and the assistant tool schema invites free-text locations ('e.g. bristol (default) or london', assistant.py input_schema). A second, stricter location-string parser exists: cli/utils.parse_location (cli/utils.py:96-142) accepts only the 'bristol' preset plus lat,lon[,alt] and raises on anything else. The web keeps its own preset table, LOCATION_PRESETS (web/shared.py:51-56), whose 'bristol' entry restates Location.bristol()'s constants. The two parsers disagree on the preset set, on altitude, and on refusal. [Also observed by web-forms:] Heuristic 10, informatively; INV-11, no silent fail-soft. resolve_location (shared.py:59-72) answers Bristol for any string that is neither a preset nor a parseable 'lat,lon'. Its docstring says so, but nothing is emitted. It is the location reader for both form parsers: parse_home_config (simulation_params.py:343, 354, after str() of whatever was sent) and parse_fleet_form (fleet_scenario.py:131). Measured: 'bristl' and '51.5,-2.6,' both run at Bristol. The assistant's run_home_simulation and run_fleet_simulation tools pass a model-chosen free-text location ("Location preset, e.g. 'bristol' (default) or 'london'", assistant.py:446, 477) through parse_home_config. So 'Cardiff' or 'London, UK' runs at Bristol while the assistant reports the requested site. builder_form._location_block refuses an unknown preset, so the dashboard already reads locations two ways. LOCATION_PRESETS['bristol'] (shared.py:51-56) also re-spells Location.bristol()'s values (heuristic 11). [Also observed by web-server:] Heuristic 10 (invariants informatively enforced) and INV-11 (no silent fail-soft): resolve_location (shared.py:59-72) turns any location it cannot read into Bristol, with no error, warning or log. That covers an unknown preset, a 'lat,lon' string that does not split into two floats, and coordinates Location() refuses. Probe: 'glasgow', 'Cardiff', '91,0', '51.5,-2.6,10' and '51.5;-2.6' all return Location(51.45, -2.58, name='Bristol, UK'), and parse_home_config({'pv_kw': 4, 'location': 'glasgow'}) builds a Bristol home. Every home config the web reads goes through it: POST /api/simulate/home, /simulate/fleet and /simulate/sweep, and both assistant trigger tools via parse_home_config (simulation_params.py:343,354), plus the fleet form via fleet_scenario._fleet_form_location (fleet_scenario.py:129-131). The assistant's tool schema invites free text ('Location preset, e.g. bristol (default) or london', assistant.py:446-449, 477-480), so a model asked for a Cardiff run submits a Bristol run and reports success. Heuristic 11: the scenario builder reads the same preset names and refuses unknown ones (builder_form.py:232-236), so one input has two policies. The same tool family also clamps n_homes to [1, 100] without saying so, and reads a non-numeric value as 1 (assistant.py:660-663). No test pins the fallback.
findings.proposal: Refuse an unrecognised location in resolve_location with a ValueError naming 'location' and the value. Every web caller already answers ValueError with HTTP 400 and the assistant with an error dict. Then share one location-string parser, presets included, between cli/utils and web/shared, defined below both. The refusal is mechanical; sharing the parser spans cli and web.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — shared.py LOCATION_PRESETS still re-spells Bristol, and resolve_location still swallows ValueError. assistant.py:446-449 and 477-480 still invite free-text locations. run_fleet_simulation still clamps n_homes silently (660-663).

findings.statement: Heuristic 9 (deep modules in strata): RunStorage reads as the owner of runs, but the runs table has five SQL clients. It is written by storage.py (upsert, labels, delete) and also by jobs.py: the submit-time INSERT with its own hand-listed 12 columns (jobs.py:427-450, while storage derives its column list from RunRecord's fields, storage.py:228-245, so a new column is a lockstep edit, INV-5), the failure UPDATE (146-158), the refused-submit DELETE (504-510) and the startup recovery UPDATE (765-774). It is read with raw SQL by api.history_list_runs (api.py:646-689), assistant.list_recent_runs (assistant.py:549-557) and routes._get_aggregate_stats (routes.py:34-58, with a 'completed' string literal in place of RunStatus and a function-local get_db import). config_presets is split the same way: presets.py owns it, yet api.py queries it raw at 955-967 and 1000-1019, where a database error is logged and answered 404 'not found'. database.py holds the schema, connections and the chat_messages store. The persistence layer is a flat mesh, not strata. Heuristic 7: JobManager.submit_home_job/submit_fleet_job require db_path and data_dir on every call (jobs.py:243-335; six call sites in api.py and assistant.py read them from app.config), and each job builds its own RunStorage (jobs.py:656, 723). dispatch_tool builds another per get_run_results call (assistant.py:732), although app.extensions['storage'] holds one. Commit 6008461 moved chat()'s run-context lookup onto the app's RunStorage for this reason and left dispatch_tool behind.
findings.proposal: Make RunStorage the only module that issues SQL against runs, and have JobManager take a RunStorage (or a narrower run-recorder interface) at construction instead of paths per submit. The rows a job writes (create queued, mark failed, recover stale) become RunStorage methods, and the list, paged-list and aggregate reads become RunStorage queries returning RunRecord. Move the scenario-preset reads into presets.py. This spans storage.py, jobs.py, api.py, assistant.py and routes.py and changes JobManager's constructor and submit signatures (web-internal, not frozen surface).
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — The raw runs SQL in jobs.py (427-450, 146-158, 504-510, 750-775), api.history_list_runs (648-689), assistant.list_recent_runs (549-557) and routes._get_aggregate_stats (34-58) is unchanged. config_presets is still read raw in api.py:956-969 and 1001-1019, outside presets.py. More evidence: scenarios_list_presets filters type = 'fleet', but scenarios_get_preset does not, so GET /api/scenarios/presets/<name> answers a saved home preset. The per-job RunStorage (jobs 656/723) and dispatch_tool's RunStorage (assistant 732) remain.

findings.statement: Heuristic 11 (SPOT): the run list is implemented three times. RunStorage.list_runs (storage.py:690-743), with type/status filters, limit and offset, is used only by routes.index (routes.py:71) and tests. history_list_runs re-implements filtering, ordering and pagination in raw SQL (api.py:646-689), and assistant.list_recent_runs does it again (assistant.py:549-557). The table projection (total_generation_kwh, self_consumption_ratio picked out of summary_json) is written twice (api.py:702-703, assistant.py:572-573). Decoding summary_json has three behaviours: RunRecord.decoded_summary falls back to {} (storage.py:206-213); api.py:697-701 copies that fallback inline; get_job_results (api.py:270) and get_run_results (assistant.py:510) call json.loads raw, so malformed text is a 500 in one and a 'Database error' dict in the other. Heuristic 8: list_runs hands back mutable untyped dicts where run_record returns the frozen RunRecord.
findings.proposal: Give RunStorage one list query (filters, search, sort whitelist, page) returning RunRecords, plus one projection helper for the list's summary metrics. Have the History API, the dashboard and the assistant tool call those, and use decoded_summary() everywhere. Spans api.py, assistant.py and storage.py; best done with the RunStorage ownership finding.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — RunStorage.list_runs (storage.py:690-743) is still used only by routes.index. api.py:646-705 and assistant.py:549-575 re-implement the listing, and the three summary decoders still behave differently.

findings.statement: Heuristic 13 (files make sense in isolation; function-local imports are a symptom): four function-local imports in the server modules break no cycle and save no cost, and each silences the lint that would flag it with # noqa: PLC0415. api.py:373 imports fleet_config inside preview_distribution, though api's own top-level import of fleet_scenario has already loaded it (verified: building the app leaves solar_challenge.web.fleet_config in sys.modules). api.py:530 imports uuid and api.py:555 imports math inside simulate_sweep. routes.py:34 imports get_db inside _get_aggregate_stats, though database is already loaded through storage. The charts deferrals (routes.py:122, 192; history.py:88) do have a reason: building the app leaves plotly unimported. The reason is recorded nowhere and pinned by no test, unlike the anthropic deferral (test_building_the_app_does_not_import_the_anthropic_sdk). web/__init__.py:15-22 is a lazy re-export shim of create_app typed as returning Any, so the CLI's app is untyped.
findings.proposal: Hoist the four no-reason imports to module level and drop their noqa. For charts, keep the deferral and pin it as the anthropic one is (a test that building the app does not import plotly), with a pointer from the import. Type web/__init__.create_app's return as Flask under TYPE_CHECKING. Mechanical.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — api.py:373 (fleet_config), 530 (uuid), 555 (math) and routes.py:34 (get_db) still have function-local imports with noqa PLC0415. The charts deferrals remain at routes.py:122/192 and history.py:88. web/__init__.py is still the lazy create_app shim returning Any.

findings.statement: Heuristic 1 (informative names): sweep_id (api.py:579, 597) is a fresh uuid4 that identifies nothing. No row, file or endpoint records it; the sweep page only displays it ('Sweep ID', templates/scenarios/sweep.html:170). Each point is stored as an ordinary 'home' run named 'Sweep <parameter>=<value>' (api.py:592). The 'sweep' member of RunType (database.py:22), which History's type filter offers (templates/history/runs.html:26), is never written by any code, so that filter always comes back empty. Heuristic 10: the 2-50 step range lives only in the page (sweep.html:55); the server checks steps >= 2 and nothing above (api.py:546-547), so one POST can submit any number of jobs, each with a runs and a jobs row.
findings.proposal: Either record the sweep (store its runs with type 'sweep' and a sweep id the History page can group by) or drop sweep_id and the dead 'sweep' RunType and filter option. Enforce the step ceiling on the server from one constant the page also renders. Mechanical within api.py, database.py and the two templates.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — sweep_id = str(_uuid.uuid4()) at api.py:579 is still recorded nowhere, and points are still named 'Sweep {parameter}={val}' as home runs (592). No writer stores RunType 'sweep' (grep of run_type= in src: only 'home' and 'fleet').

findings.statement: Tests stance and heuristic 7: create_app takes only a config mapping, so there is no seam to give the app a JobManager (or the simulate_home a JobManager accepts). Tests reach into the composition root's wiring instead: they overwrite app.extensions['job_manager'] after construction at 12 sites (tests/unit/web_api/conftest.py:71, test_web_jobs.py:144, test_web_jobs_drain_scope.py:31, web_api/test_simulate_sweep.py:50, web_assistant/test_tool_use.py:660/737/812, test_cli_web.py:42, e2e/conftest.py:155-161 swapping it mid-session, and others). That orphans the real manager create_app built and registered with atexit. Production reads the same untyped string keys through shared.get_storage/get_job_manager, each with a type: ignore[no-any-return] (shared.py:15-22), a heuristic 12 smell. No test patches a _-prefixed name of the ten server modules by dotted path or reads their private attributes (grep over tests/: none). The JobManager doubles in the pinned tree are MagicMock(spec=JobManager) or plain MagicMock (tool_use tests). The task-682 autospec doubles landed after the pin and also stay on the public interface. The reach is into the app's wiring key, not JobManager internals.
findings.proposal: Give create_app an explicit, typed collaborator parameter (e.g. job_manager: JobManager | None, or a simulate_home), and store the collaborators in one typed holder rather than string-keyed extensions. Then move the 12 test sites onto the constructor seam. Changes create_app's signature (web-internal, not frozen surface) and touches the test fixtures.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — create_app(test_config) still has no JobManager parameter (app.py:63-148). grep of tests/ for extensions['job_manager'] = gives 10 assignment sites. shared.get_storage/get_job_manager still carry type: ignore[no-any-return].

findings.statement: Heuristics 11 and 12: each tool's name is written in TOOLS (assistant.py:321-486) and again in dispatch_tool's string if-chain (720-742), with ad hoc input coercion per branch (str(), float(), int() with silent defaults). Heuristic 3: each tool's schema and its handler live in different places, so adding or renaming one is a lockstep edit in two places, and a third: the literal name list in test_tool_use.py:77-84. A mismatch is found only at runtime, as the model receiving an 'Unknown tool' error dict. Six stable tools in a frozen-posture repo keep the cost low.
findings.proposal: Declare each tool once as a (schema, input reader, handler) record, derive TOOLS from the records in their fixed order, and dispatch through a name-to-record mapping. Stays in assistant.py.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — assistant.py:720-744 is still a string if-chain over the six names that TOOLS (321-486) also lists.

findings.statement: Heuristic 5 (minimum data scopes and lifetimes): jobs.py keeps a module-level WeakSet of every JobManager (_active_managers, jobs.py:48), filled by every constructor (215). Its only consumers are the CLI, whose 'web start' calls shutdown_all_managers() (cli/web.py:62) although it holds the app that owns the manager, and tests/conftest.py's autouse fixture. Heuristic 11: a second, ineffective shutdown mechanism also exists. create_app registers atexit.register(job_manager.shutdown) (app.py:135), but JobManager.shutdown's own docstring says that by the time atexit hooks run, concurrent.futures has already run every queued job. A probe confirms it: four queued jobs on a one-worker executor all ran before an atexit shutdown(cancel_futures=True). The hook also holds a strong reference to every manager create_app builds, so the 'weak' registry never drops one, including the managers tests orphan by swapping app.extensions['job_manager']. app.py's __main__ path (application.run(debug=True)) has only the ineffective hook.
findings.proposal: Own the lifecycle where the app is built: give create_app (or a small app-scoped object it returns) an explicit shutdown that the CLI and the test fixtures call. Delete the atexit registration and the module-level registry. This changes the contract between cli/web.py, app.py, jobs.py and tests/conftest.py.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — The module WeakSet _active_managers (jobs.py:48) and its add in __init__ (215) are unchanged. cli/web.py still calls shutdown_all_managers() in finally (cli/web.py file line 62), and app.py:135 still registers atexit.register(job_manager.shutdown).

findings.statement: config.py's distribution grammar reads numbers with bare float()/int(). config.py::_build_normal_spec calls float(data['mean']), _build_weighted_discrete_spec calls float(w), and _build_shuffled_pool_spec calls int(c), which truncates 2.5 and raises OverflowError on inf. parse_fleet_distribution_config truncates n_homes with int() and takes seed unchecked. NormalDistribution, UniformDistribution and ShuffledPoolDistribution.__post_init__ check ordering and sign but not finiteness. Because of this, every web entry point must pre-read every number through number_fields before config sees it. To reach those numbers, fleet_config.py::_parse_component_distribution walks and rebuilds each block through _build_distribution_dict and _other_setting. The rebuild is lossy and re-decides what config already decides; all of the following was run at the pin: (a) pv.capacity_kw {type: normal, mena: 4, std: 1} becomes {type: normal, mean: 0.0, std: 1.0}, and config accepts N(0,1), because the misspelt key never reaches config's _refuse_unrecognised_keys. (b) pv.tilt {type: fixed, value: 30} and battery.max_charge_kw {type: proportional_to, source: battery.capacity_kwh, multiplier: 0.5} are both valid in config's grammar, but they are cut down to {type: ...} and refused with "requires 'value'" or "requires 'source'", naming a key the user did send. (c) _spec_number invents defaults that config's grammar refuses as missing: mean 0, std 1, uniform 0..1, weight 1, count 1. fleet_scenario::_read_fleet_size_and_seed exists only to run 'ahead of the loaders, whose int() would refuse n_homes first'. Each new entry point repeats the pre-read or forgets it: api.py::simulate_sweep still uses bare float()/int(), and assistant.py reads n_homes with int().
findings.proposal: Give the number invariant one home in config.py. Add _finite_number(value, path) and _whole_count(value, path, low=0), built on whole_numbers.whole_number; they refuse bool, NaN, inf and fractions with a ConfigurationError naming the path. Call them from every _build_*_spec, from _parse_distribution_spec's scalar branch, and from parse_fleet_distribution_config for n_homes and seed. Repeat the finiteness check in the __post_init__ of NormalDistribution, UniformDistribution, WeightedDiscreteDistribution and ShuffledPoolDistribution, so it is enforced at both construction and parse (heuristic 10, redundant). This refuses NaN for the downstream consumer too, which is intended. Apply the dashboard-only bounds (MAX_FLEET_HOMES on n_homes and on pool totals) once, to the parsed FleetDistributionConfig, not to the raw dict. The web layer can then pass blocks through as sent, so config's unrecognised-key and presence rules see what the user posted. What becomes deletable: fleet_config._other_setting, _spec_number and the _is_fixed_value branch of _parse_component_distribution; the read_fleet_size/read_fleet_seed pre-reads; fleet_scenario._read_fleet_size_and_seed's ordering hack; and FLEET_FORM_REFUSALS' need to list ValueError. This would have prevented 312, 441, 498, 520, the 509 class of dropped or ignored keys, and the strip bugs that 519 and 535 patched one shape at a time.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — Probed at pin: pv.capacity_kw {type: normal, mena: 4, std: 1} -> {type: normal, mean: 0.0, std: 1.0} and parse_fleet_distribution_config accepts N(0,1); pv.tilt {type: fixed, value: 30} refused 'requires value'; {type: normal} -> mean 0 std 1. api.py simulate_sweep still float(data.get('min'))/int(data.get('steps')).

findings.statement: Both fleet pages edit a component through one editor state, fleet_components.py::EditorDistribution.editor_state and distribution-editor.js, but each page serialises it into its own wire grammar. fleet-simulator.js _buildDistPayload posts a nested body: {pv: {capacity_kw: {type, mean, ..., values: [{value, weight}], entries: [{value, count}]}}}. scenario-builder.js componentFormData flattens the same state to pv_distribution_type, pv_mean, pv_wd_values and pv_sp_entries. Two server decoders then turn these into config's grammar under different rules. fleet_config.py::_build_distribution_dict defaults absent parameters, bounds pool counts by MAX_FLEET_HOMES through _pool_counts, and returns a bare {type} for a type it does not know. builder_form.py::_distribution_spec leaves absent parameters out for the loader to refuse, reads counts through as_whole_number with no bound, and refuses an unknown type itself. Verified at the pin: the builder's {type: normal, mean: 4} is refused by the loader ("requires 'mean' and 'std'"), while the fleet page's {type: normal} runs as N(0,1). The component keys are restated as well. FLEET_COMPONENTS already carries grammar_key, yet fleet_config::form_to_fleet_distribution_config and fleet_scenario::_read_fleet_distribution/_read_battery hard-code 'capacity_kw', 'capacity_kwh' and 'annual_consumption_kwh'. Every distribution rule is therefore decided twice on the server, and a third time in each page's JS.
findings.proposal: Make the editor state the one wire shape. A module web/editor_distribution.py, or methods on EditorDistribution, would provide three things. read_editor_distribution(obj, path) is the one reader of an editor dist's numbers and rows (finite floats, whole bounded counts). to_grammar_spec() returns config's spec, and from_grammar_spec(spec, path) is its inverse. Both pages post {component.key: <editor dist>} exactly as the editor holds it. Server loops iterate FLEET_COMPONENTS and use grammar_key, never literals. What becomes deletable: fleet-simulator.js::_buildDistPayload/_distFromConfig and scenario-builder.js::componentFormData; builder_form._DISTRIBUTION_FIELDS, _prefixed, _distribution_spec and _row_lists; fleet_config._build_distribution_dict, _named_rows, _spec_number and _pool_counts; and distribution_form_spec/_form_numbers/_form_number_list/_form_count_list, which become the module's inverse. This would have prevented 313 (two writers disagree), 553 and 561, the restated-keys half of 566 and 611, and the unbounded builder pool below.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — Probed: builder {pv_distribution_type: normal, pv_mean: 4} -> {type: normal, mean: 4.0} (no std, left for loader to refuse) vs fleet {type: normal} -> N(0,1). form_to_fleet_distribution_config still hard-codes 'capacity_kw'/'capacity_kwh'/'annual_consumption_kwh'; fleet_scenario._read_fleet_distribution/_read_battery likewise.

findings.statement: builder_form.py::_distribution_spec reads shuffled_pool counts with as_whole_number, which has no bound, and _dashboard_limit_errors checks no count. Verified at the pin: scenario_from_builder_form accepts {n_homes: 10, pv_distribution_type: shuffled_pool, pv_sp_entries: [{value: 4, count: 10**12}]}, and the dashboard limits report no error. builder_form_errors then runs load_fleet_config on that document, since n_homes is within bounds. The path continues through generate_homes_from_distribution and _DistributionSampler.prepare to ShuffledPoolDistribution.create_pool, which builds [4.0] * 10**12 inside the request thread of POST /api/scenarios/validate, exhausting memory. Commit de19110 (fix 312) says 'so no route builds an unbounded pool', but it bounded only fleet_config._pool_counts, which the builder route never reaches.
findings.proposal: Immediate fix: read builder counts through the same bounded rule, by sharing fleet_config._pool_counts or calling as_whole_number_within(count, field, 0, MAX_FLEET_HOMES) plus a total check, so validate refuses before load_fleet_config runs. Structural fix: the single editor-distribution decoder in the finding above. Also bound the pool total against n_homes in config itself, so no caller can build a pool larger than the fleet.
findings.verdict_notes: still_present — Probed scenario_from_builder_form with pv_sp_entries count 10**12 -> counts [1000000000000]; _dashboard_limit_errors returns []. _row_lists still reads counts with unbounded as_whole_number (did not run the loader, which would build the pool).

findings.statement: fleet_config.py::_draw_samples re-implements config's _sample_from_distribution and _DistributionSampler, and re-checks only some of the distribution invariants.
